title: Information, partnership and shared decision making
blurb: Share information about conditions and treatments clearly, explain risks well and make decisions with people, not for them.
question: A patient asks whether a new medicine will 'halve' his risk of a stroke. The risk falls from 2 in 100 to 1 in 100 over five years. How should the nurse explain this?

teach.body: NICE defines shared decision making as a collaborative process in which a person and their healthcare professional work together to reach a joint decision about care. Plain English: you bring the clinical knowledge, they bring what matters in their life, and you decide together. The Code asks you to work in partnership (2.1), encourage and empower people to share decisions (2.3) and respect how involved each person wants to be (2.4).

teach.h: Before, during and after the discussion (NG197)

teach.caption: Pictures such as icon arrays help people see both positive and negative framing at once.

teach.h: Information before, during and after care
teach.body: Explain the condition, what an intervention involves, the risks, benefits and consequences of each option (including doing nothing), and what to expect afterwards. Discuss risks that are common, those that are serious even if rare, and those the person is likely to think important. Check understanding, give time, and make clear they can change their mind at any time.
teach.cite: NICE NG197 1.2.10–1.2.16; NMC/GMC candour guidance para 8; Montgomery (2015)

teach.h: Three questions people are encouraged to ask

letters.word: What are the Benefits and risks?

teach.h: Worked scenario: Practice Nurse Leo at a GP surgery
teach.body: Mr Adeyemi, 66, is offered a medicine to lower his stroke risk. Leo asks what matters most to him: staying active for his grandchildren. Leo explains that over five years, about 2 in 100 people like him would have a stroke without the medicine and about 1 in 100 with it, and that some people get side effects. They agree he will try it for three months and review, and Leo records the decision and what mattered to him.

teach.caption: Code 2.2: recognise and respect the contribution people can make to their own health and wellbeing.

items: Agree shared goals that reflect what matters to the person (P3.4).
Teach skills in small steps and check with teach-back.
Give written or digital resources in their preferred format, with who to contact.
Involve family, friends or carers if the person wishes.
Agree when to review, and that they can review sooner if they want.

teach.text: 'Halves your risk' is RELATIVE risk and sounds bigger than it is. NG197 says use ABSOLUTE risk: '2 in 100 become 1 in 100 over five years'.

items: Shared decision making: a joint decision that reflects what matters to the person.
Discuss all options including no treatment; give time; agree a review; they can change their mind.
Risks: absolute numbers, natural frequencies, same denominator, both framings, a timescale.
Record the decision and what mattered to the person, and share it with them.

summary: You can now share information about conditions and treatments clearly, present risks in the way NICE recommends and reach joint decisions with people. You can also use strength-based approaches to support people to manage their own health.

A.q: According to NICE NG197, which is the best way to describe a risk to a patient?
options: 'This treatment cuts your risk of a stroke by 50%.'
'Side effects from this medicine are rare.'
'About 3 in 100 people get this side effect in a year.'
'Most people are absolutely fine taking it.'
A.why: NG197 recommends numerical data as natural frequencies (3 in 100) over a defined time period, rather than words like 'rare' or relative risk.

whyNot.0: A relative risk reduction can exaggerate benefit; absolute risk is preferred.
whyNot.1: People interpret words like 'rare' in different ways.
whyNot.3: This is vague and gives only a positive framing.

A.q: When discussing treatment options, which must the nurse make sure the person knows is also an option?
options: Choosing no treatment or no change
Asking a relative to decide
Choosing the cheapest option
Delaying until symptoms worsen
A.why: NG197 1.2.10: discuss the risks, benefits and consequences of each option, making sure the person knows this includes choosing no treatment or no change.

whyNot.1: The decision belongs to the person, though they can involve others if they wish.
whyNot.2: Cost is not an option the nurse is required to present.
whyNot.3: Waiting for deterioration is not a recommended option to offer.

A.q: Which Code standard asks nurses to encourage and empower people to share decisions about their treatment and care?
A.why: Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions about their treatment and care.

whyNot.0: 2.6 is responding compassionately to anxiety or distress.
whyNot.1: 2.1 is working in partnership to deliver care effectively.
whyNot.2: 2.4 is respecting how far people want to be involved.

B.q: A patient has agreed to start home oxygen. At the end of the discussion, what does NG197 recommend the nurse does?
options: Ask the patient to sign a consent form for oxygen
Summarise what was agreed, next steps and the review date
Send the summary to the GP rather than the patient
Let the patient reflect overnight before summarising
B.why: NG197 1.2.15: at the end of a discussion, state clearly what decisions have been made, what happens next, the timescales and when it will be reviewed.

whyNot.0: A signature is not the NG197 recommendation for ending a discussion.
whyNot.2: The patient should receive the summary; letters go to the patient with a copy to the GP.
whyNot.3: Leaving without a summary risks misunderstanding.

B.q: Two treatments carry side effect risks of 1 in 14 and 1 in 5. How should the nurse present them, following NG197?
options: As 7% and 20%
As 'uncommon' and 'common'
As 1 in 14 and 1 in 5
As 7 in 100 and 20 in 100
B.why: NG197 1.4.9: use the same denominator when comparing risks, such as 7 in 100 and 20 in 100.

whyNot.0: NG197 prefers natural frequencies to percentages.
whyNot.1: Words like 'common' are interpreted differently by different people.

B.q: A woman with diabetes says she wants to manage her own insulin but feels unsure. Which response reflects a strength-based approach?
options: 'Let's build on what you already do well and plan next steps.'
'The community nurse can give your injections for you instead.'
'Your daughter should take charge of your insulin from now on.'
'You may find it too difficult to manage at your age.'
B.why: Strength-based approaches build on the person's abilities and goals and support self-management (P2.9, P4.2; Code 2.2).

whyNot.1: Taking over removes her chance to self-manage.
whyNot.2: This transfers control without her agreement.

C.q: Mr Clarke, who has capacity, chooses a treatment option that the nurse thinks is less effective, because it lets him keep working. What should the nurse do?
options: Persuade him to switch to the more effective option instead
Ask his wife to help him change his mind about it
Accept his view, record what mattered and agree a review
Refer him for a formal mental capacity assessment
C.why: NG197 1.2.13 asks professionals to accept that people may weigh risks and benefits differently; 1.2.17 asks for decisions and what mattered to be recorded.

whyNot.0: Pressuring him undermines a shared decision.
whyNot.1: Involving others to change his mind is not partnership.
whyNot.3: A different view of risk is not a reason to doubt capacity.

C.q: A nurse is preparing a patient for a colonoscopy. When should she give information about what the procedure involves and what to expect afterwards?
options: During the procedure, so it is fresh in mind
Before, during and after the procedure
After the procedure, once sedation has worn off
Whenever the patient asks for it
C.why: P4.3: provide accurate information before, during and after interventions, so people know what to expect and can make informed choices.

whyNot.0: Information given only during the procedure is too late for an informed decision.
whyNot.2: Giving information only afterwards means consent was not informed.
whyNot.3: Information should be offered, not left for the patient to request.

C.q: A patient decision aid is used during a discussion about knee surgery. Which statement about decision aids is correct?
options: They help people weigh options but do not recommend one
They tell people which option is best for them
They replace the discussion with a professional
They are suitable whether or not quality assured
C.why: NG197: patient decision aids help people think about options and what matters to them; they do not advise one option, nor replace consultation, and should be quality assured.

whyNot.1: Decision aids do not advise people to choose one option.
whyNot.2: They support, not replace, the professional discussion.
whyNot.3: NG197 1.3.2: use decision aids that are quality assured.

reteach.title: Two experts in the room
reteach.question: Who is the expert on what matters in the patient's life?

blocks.body: You are the expert on the condition and the options. The person is the expert on their life, values and goals. Shared decision making puts both kinds of expertise on the table: you explain options and risks clearly, they say what matters, and together you agree a plan you will both review.

blocks.text: Shared decision making is not handing over a leaflet and asking for a signature. It is a conversation with options, risks in numbers and time to decide.

explain.body: Prepare people before the discussion, agree an agenda, discuss options including no treatment, chunk and check, decide together and agree a review.

test.q: What does NG197 recommend at the start of each shared decision-making discussion?
options: Hand over a consent form
Give a full list of side effects
Ask the family to leave
Agree an agenda and its length
test.why: NG197 1.2.7: agree an 'agenda' at the start of each discussion to prioritise what to discuss, and say how long it will last.

whyNot.0: Consent forms are not the starting point of the discussion.
whyNot.1: Information is shared through the discussion in manageable chunks.
whyNot.2: The person may choose to involve family.

explain.body: Use absolute risk, natural frequencies, the same denominator, both framings and a time period; add pictures where helpful.

test.q: A treatment reduces a risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. Which description follows NG197?
options: 'It halves your risk of this happening.'
'It makes the treatment 50% safer for you.'
'The risk goes from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000.'
'The risk becomes very small indeed for you.'
test.why: NG197 1.4.7: use absolute risk rather than relative risk.

whyNot.1: A percentage reduction is relative risk.

explain.body: Record the decision and what mattered to the person, share it with them, and remind them they can review it earlier or change their mind.

test.q: What should be recorded after a shared decision, according to NG197?
options: The decision and the nurse's opinion of it
The decision and what mattered to the person
The options the patient turned down
A note that the patient was compliant
test.why: NG197 1.2.17: record any decisions made along with details of what the person said was important to them, and offer to share this.

whyNot.0: The nurse's opinion is not what NG197 asks to be recorded.
whyNot.2: The decision itself must be recorded.
whyNot.3: 'Compliant' does not record the decision or the person's priorities.

explain.body: Start from what the person can do, agree shared goals and support them to manage their own health.

test.q: Which Code standard asks nurses to recognise and respect the contribution people can make to their own health and wellbeing?
test.why: Code 2.2: recognise and respect the contribution that people can make to their own health and wellbeing.

whyNot.1: 2.5 is respecting the right to accept or refuse care.
whyNot.2: 3.3 is helping people access health and social care and information.
